chapters.title: Why it really ended (your side of it)
chapters.teaser: Not who was right. What your soul was doing while it fell apart.

chapters.title: Your breakup pattern
chapters.teaser: How you end things, how you grieve, and the habit that slows you down.

chapters.title: Why you keep checking
chapters.teaser: What the pull back toward them is really asking for.

chapters.title: So, will they come back? The honest answer
chapters.teaser: What a chart can and can't tell you, and the question that matters more.

chapters.title: If they ever reach out
chapters.teaser: Three questions to ask before you reply, built for your soul.

chapters.title: What you do now
chapters.teaser: The next small steps that help, whatever they decide.

text.why-it-ended: Gi Earth is the garden: soft soil, generous, the place where things grow. You probably nurtured that relationship like something you loved tending. You remembered their appointments, handled the logistics, smoothed out their stress. Gardens give without asking, which is beautiful, and it can quietly turn you into the caretaker instead of the partner. Maybe they got comfortable and stopped tending you back. Maybe you got so busy keeping things alive that you forgot to check whether you still wanted to be there. Either way, the ending probably followed a long season of you giving more than you received.
text.your-breakup-pattern: After a breakup you worry. About them, about what you did wrong, about practical things like who keeps the plant. Gi Earth thinks in details and responsibilities. Your pattern is taking more than your share of the blame, because if it was your fault, you can fix it, and fixing feels better than helplessness. It's also usually not accurate. Two people built that garden. Your other pattern: you look after everyone around you through the heartbreak and forget to feed yourself. Let someone else bring the soup this time. Then actually eat it.
text.the-pull: The thing that pulls you back is the investment. You put so much care in that walking away feels wasteful. You might also worry that they can't cope without you. Gi Earth loves being needed, and a breakup takes that role away overnight. Notice the difference between missing them and missing being useful to them. Both are real, but only one needs them specifically. Your care has plenty of places to go: a friend who's struggling, a project, a pet, your own future. Plant something new. Even a literal one, on the windowsill, is a decent start.
text.the-honest-answer: No chart can tell you what another person will choose. That belongs to them. What we can see is how you love: practically, generously, sometimes to the point of disappearing. If you're hoping they come back, picture the relationship continuing exactly as it was. Would you still be the one managing everything? If yes, wanting them back may really be wanting your effort to finally be seen. That's a fair wish, and you can give yourself some of that recognition today. Write down what you gave. It was a lot. It counted, even if nobody said thank you.
text.if-they-reach-out: If they ever write, you'll want to help with whatever they need. Pause. Ask what you need first. Gi Earth slides back into caretaking almost on autopilot. Before replying, choose one boundary: maybe you won't be their emotional support while they work things out, or you'll only meet if they've actually thought about what went wrong. Then see how they respond to it. A reconnection that's good for you feels mutual from the very first conversation. If it already feels like work in that first exchange, believe it. That feeling is information, not impatience.
text.what-you-do-now: Tend your own garden. Gi Earth is brilliant at care, so aim it home. Cook proper meals for yourself. Make your space cozy. Keep a simple routine that feels good, not one that's productive for everyone else. Let friends look after you and resist the urge to repay them immediately. Spend time with people who ask how you are and wait for the answer. And practice small selfish choices: the film you want, the restaurant you like. You've been fertile ground for everyone around you. You get to grow something for yourself now.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You took such good care of them, Gi. That was love.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: It was also unpaid management. Did they ever water you back?

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: It wasn't all your fault. Two people built that garden.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Stop taking the blame just because it feels like control.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Let someone bring you soup this time.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Plant something new. A tomato. A hobby. Not them, by reflex.

spring.intro: Spring soil gets dug up, planted in and asked to feed everything. Your birth season belonged to Wood, Gi, and Wood controls Earth, so you grew up making room for other people's growth. In love that means you nurtured: their plans, their confidence, their moods. You were the field they grew in. After a breakup, soil like yours often feels depleted and strangely guilty, as if a failed harvest were your fault. It wasn't. Some seeds don't take, however good the ground. The pull back may be the urge to keep tending something already gone. Give yourself a fallow season. Fields that rest grow better crops, and the next one should be yours.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Good soil doesn't owe anyone a harvest. Rest, Gi. You've earned it.

summer.intro: Summer soil is warm, rich and ready. Your season belonged to Fire, Gi, and Fire feeds Earth, so your chart is nourished and steady at its core. You love practically and generously, and you probably held the relationship together in a hundred small ways nobody counted. The risk for well-fed Gi is that you also absorb a lot: their stress, their silences, their version of the breakup. You might still be carrying feelings that were never yours. Before asking whether they'll return, sort through what you're holding. Which feelings belong to you, and which came with them? Soil can be generous and still have edges. Your warm season means you recover well once you put down what isn't yours.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Half the sadness you're carrying is theirs. Return to sender, Gi.

autumn.intro: Autumn is harvest, and Gi Earth is the field being harvested. Your birth season belonged to Metal, and Earth gives birth to Metal, so your chart spends itself on output: care, competence, keeping everyone fed. In the relationship you probably handled much of the emotional logistics. Who's upset, who needs what, what's for dinner. When it ended, the work stopped, and that silence is loud. Some of the pull back is genuinely missing them. Some is missing being useful. Those need different answers. The first heals with time. The second heals when you let someone take care of you without earning it first. Start with a friend who'll cook for you.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Missing them and missing being needed are not the same feeling.

winter.intro: Winter soil is cold, wet and resting. Your season belonged to Water, Gi, and Earth controls Water, so you carry a lot of feeling and work hard to keep it shaped and useful. In love you probably absorbed tension until the ground went muddy. You may have smoothed things over for so long that the breakup surprised everyone, including you. Winter Gi tends to process slowly, in private, and then suddenly understand everything one ordinary Tuesday. Give that Tuesday room. Don't rush to a conclusion, and don't let checking their profile become a way to manage feelings you'd rather not feel. Fire is your friend here: warmth, sunlight, someone who makes you laugh out loud.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You'll understand it all one ordinary day. No need to force it.

earth.intro: The Earth days are your home weather, Gi. You were born when the season hands over to soil, so your own element runs deep in you. In the relationship you were the garden: you fed, you tended, you made things grow, including them. After the breakup, the pull back is caretaking. You still wonder if they're eating properly, if they're okay, if they've worked it out. Your care is real, but it doesn't have to have their name on it. Plant something you'll get to see bloom yourself.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You can stop watering their garden, Gi. Yours has been waiting.

strength.strong: Your soil is rich and well fed, Gi. Lots of Earth and Fire in your chart make you capable, nurturing and confident in your way of caring. In love you probably ran a lot: the plans, the home, the emotional weather. The blind spot is that well-meant tending can feel like management. Your ex may have felt cared for and also slightly handled. If you're thinking about them, ask whether you miss the person or the role of looking after them. Strong soil can let someone grow wild for a season. Not everything needs your rows.
strength.weak: With little support in your chart, Gi, you give from soil that's already thin. In love you probably fed them first and yourself last, and called it kindness. It was kind. It was also costly. After the breakup you may feel wrung out and slightly ashamed of how much you gave. Don't be. Generosity isn't a mistake. Giving without being given back to is the part to change. Start small: accept help, say no once a week, let someone plan for you. Rich soil gets made by what goes into it.

balance_text.too_much_wood: Too much Wood means you push for growth and answers, even in heartbreak. You want a plan for getting over it, maybe even a plan for getting them back. Slow down. Not everything grows on schedule, and some things need to just sit for a while. Ask for help instead of turning healing into a project. For balance, let a little Metal in: declutter, finish old things, clear out the drafts folder. A clean edge helps Wood stop reaching for what's already gone.
balance_text.missing_wood: Missing Wood means fresh starts feel heavy. After a breakup you might stay in the same place, emotionally and literally, for longer than you'd like. That isn't weakness. It just means new growth needs a nudge. Small steps work best: a new route to work, one new class, one new person a week. Get outside in the mornings and keep something green near you. You don't need a whole new life. You need one new branch, and then another.
balance_text.too_much_fire: Too much Fire makes you feel everything at full volume. A breakup can feel like an emergency, with urges to text, post, or fix it all tonight. Your passion is real, but heat isn't a strategy. Before any big move, sleep on it. Cool down with water: swimming, long showers, quiet evenings at home. Talk to your calmest friend before your most exciting one. Let the fire warm you instead of burning through your peace.
balance_text.missing_fire: Missing Fire means joy and visibility don't come easily, and after a breakup you might go dim for a while, hiding from people and from fun. Turn the lights back on gently. Sunshine, music, dancing in the kitchen, one social plan a week even when you'd rather stay in. Letting people see you is the medicine here. Warmth doesn't only live in romance. It's in friends, in laughter, in simply being out in the world.
balance_text.too_much_earth: Too much Earth means you hold on: to routines, to memories, to the hope that things will settle back into their old place. Stability is your gift, but in heartbreak it can turn into staying stuck. Shake the ground a little. Move the furniture, take a short trip, try something unplanned. Let some Wood energy in, growth and new beginnings. You can keep what was good and still leave room for something new to grow.
balance_text.missing_earth: Missing Earth means life can feel unsteady, and a breakup can knock away what little ground you had. You might feel scattered, unsure where to put your feet. Build structure gently: regular meals, a steady bedtime, one place at home that's only yours. Cook something. Walk somewhere. Lean on the people who are reliable. Stability first, big decisions later. You need solid ground under you before deciding anything about the past.
balance_text.too_much_metal: Too much Metal makes you sharp and decisive, sometimes too quickly. You may have cut the relationship off cleanly and then refused to look at what you feel. Or you judge yourself harshly for every mistake you made in it. Soften the edges. Let Water in: rest, tears, music, journaling. Feeling the grief isn't the same as reopening the door. You can keep your boundaries firm and still let your heart thaw.
balance_text.missing_metal: Missing Metal means boundaries are hard, so after a breakup you might keep the door half open, answer every message, or stay friends when it hurts. Practice clean edges. Mute without guilt. Box up their things. Say no without explaining. White and silver, tidy spaces and finished tasks all help your chart. A boundary isn't cold. It's how you protect the part of you that's still healing.
balance_text.too_much_water: Too much Water means you think and feel deeply, maybe endlessly. After a breakup you might drift through memories, analyze every detail, and lose sleep to what-ifs. Your intuition is a gift, but it needs riverbanks. Add some Earth: routines, cooking, walks, people who ground you. Give overthinking a time limit. Feel it fully, then get up and do one ordinary thing.
balance_text.missing_water: Missing Water means rest and reflection get skipped. You may rush past the breakup, staying busy so you never have to sit with it. That works until suddenly it doesn't. Build in quiet on purpose: slow mornings, water by your bed, writing for five minutes at night, a bath instead of another plan. Let yourself feel without fixing. Intuition grows when you give it some silence.

too_much_wood.speaker: yeon
too_much_wood.text: So much Wood. You've drafted three versions of 'hey, random but' already.

too_much_wood.speaker: bom
too_much_wood.text: That growing energy wants a goal. Give it your own plans, not their inbox.

too_much_fire.speaker: yeon
too_much_fire.text: Too much Fire: every feeling is a five-alarm emergency. It's a breakup, not an inferno.

too_much_fire.speaker: bom
too_much_fire.text: Your passion is beautiful. Let it cool before you hit send on anything.

too_much_earth.speaker: yeon
too_much_earth.text: Heavy Earth. You'd still be in that relationship purely out of habit.

too_much_earth.speaker: bom
too_much_earth.text: Your loyalty is rare. Just make sure you're loyal to yourself too.

too_much_metal.speaker: yeon
too_much_metal.text: Lots of Metal. You cut them off cleanly, then reread everything at midnight.

too_much_metal.speaker: bom
too_much_metal.text: Being firm protected you. Being gentle with yourself will heal you.

too_much_water.speaker: yeon
too_much_water.text: Overflowing Water: you've cried to three songs and written a novel in your notes app.

too_much_water.speaker: bom
too_much_water.text: Feeling deeply is a gift. Just come up for air sometimes.

missing_wood.speaker: bom
missing_wood.text: Missing Wood can make moving on feel stuck. Small new routines count as growth.

missing_wood.speaker: yeon
missing_wood.text: You haven't changed anything since the breakup, including your lock screen. Start there.

missing_fire.speaker: bom
missing_fire.text: Missing Fire can make joy feel far away. Borrow some from a loud friend.

missing_fire.speaker: yeon
missing_fire.text: You stopped having fun when they left. Fun was never theirs to take.

missing_earth.speaker: bom
missing_earth.text: Missing Earth can make everything feel unsteady. Simple routines will hold you.

missing_earth.speaker: yeon
missing_earth.text: No Earth, no anchor. You re-decide whether to text them every hour.

missing_metal.speaker: bom
missing_metal.text: Missing Metal makes boundaries tricky. You're allowed to say no to your own phone.

missing_metal.speaker: yeon
missing_metal.text: No Metal means you'll answer at 2am. Put the phone in another room.

missing_water.speaker: bom
missing_water.text: Missing Water can make grief hide. It's okay to let it surface slowly.

missing_water.speaker: yeon
missing_water.text: You said you're fine twelve times today. Water would like a word.

gap-wood.title: Rooted in the same garden
gap-wood.text: You took care of a tree, and for a long time it felt like the best kind of work. Your Gap Wood ex had direction, a plan, a backbone, and you had the warmth that made their big ideas feel livable. You checked if they'd eaten. You asked about the meeting. They told you all about it, in detail, and then forgot to ask back. You didn't mind at first. Then you minded a little, quietly. You absorbed their stress, worried about your own things alone, and said 'I'm fine' so often it became furniture. When you finally said how tired you were, it came out bigger than you meant, and they looked hurt, as if you'd been hiding a second life. In a way you had. It was close to right, and you can feel how close, which is its own kind of grief. Being needed by them felt like being important. But being needed isn't the same as being asked. Practice the unprompted ask: tell one person this week what you need before you're exhausted. Watch how much less it costs early.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gi, you were the soil. Soil is allowed to ask for rain.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: For Gap, 'how was your day' was four words. There were years to say them.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: A strong match still needs both people talking. Keep that lesson close.

eul-wood.title: The vine in the garden bed
eul-wood.text: You gave a vine everything it needed to grow, and it grew, and you got smaller. Your Eul Wood ex was charming, social, emotionally fluent in a way you're not always. They sent feelings; you sent questions. 'Did you eat?' 'Did you book it?' Your care came as logistics, theirs came as fun, and somewhere along the way the logistics stopped being answered. When you worried, they told you you were overthinking, which made you feel silly for caring at all. You didn't argue. You absorbed. You composted the resentment into more helpfulness, and eventually there was nothing left to give. This is the quiet kind of hurt: feeling taken for granted by someone you'd never call cruel. They made you laugh, and that's what you miss. With them you were lighter than you are alone. Watch for the moment you start a sentence with 'I'll just do it'. Stop right there. Let something sit undone, or ask someone else. You are allowed to be soil that also gets watered.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gi, you're not 'too much' for worrying. You care in practical ways.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Someone kept Eul fed for months. Was there a thank you?

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Who gets the nutrients? Next time, both of you.

byeong-fire.title: Sun on the garden, nobody watering
byeong-fire.text: You were the soil under someone's sunshine, and you did so much invisible work it became the background of the relationship. Your Byeong Fire ex was warm and generous and constantly forgetting things. You remembered. The errand, the call to their mom, the bill. You asked questions; they answered with emojis and enthusiasm and half the information. When you worried, they told you to relax, which felt like being told your care was a mood problem. You started feeling like the grown-up in a house with a very charming teenager. And because you avoid conflict, you didn't say it until you were too tired to say it nicely. The warmth was real, and you were still exhausted. Both things are true. Their brightness tugs at you. With them, you laughed more and worried less, at least sometimes. Let something go unchecked this week. A bill can be paid tomorrow. A plan can slip without you catching it. Watch how the world mostly holds. You don't have to audit the sunshine to deserve it.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gi, you're allowed to stop managing and just enjoy the sun.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Byeong forgetting the errand once was cute. Forty times was a pattern.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Things grew here. That part was real.

jeong-fire.title: Candlelight in the kitchen, worrying
jeong-fire.text: You looked after someone whose worries lived in a different room from yours. Your Jeong Fire ex worried about feelings: 'are we okay?', 'are you upset?', 'you seem off'. You worried about practical things: rent, dinner, whether they'd slept. You answered their emotional questions with care in the form of tasks, and they kept asking, because it wasn't the answer they needed. They felt you were focused on chores. You felt they were focused on moods. And because neither of you likes confrontation, the tension stayed under the surface, warm but uneasy. It hurts to feel that your care didn't count, as if feeding someone well wasn't love. It was. It was just a dialect they didn't speak. Their warmth tugs. They noticed your heart in a way practical people rarely get noticed. When someone asks 'are we okay?', start with the feeling. 'Yes, I love you. Also, did you eat?' Lead with the answer to their question, then ask yours.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gi, 'did you eat?' is love. Say 'I love you' first, though.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Jeong's 'are we okay' forty times a week was a symptom, not a question.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Answer what they're actually asking. Then ask your own.

mu-earth.title: Mountain and valley
mu-earth.text: You loved a mountain, and it was safe and solid and not much of a talker. Your Mu Earth ex was dependable in every practical way. But when you worried, they said 'don't worry', which felt like being dismissed. When you asked how their day went, you got a short, solid answer and no question back. You did the invisible work, all of it, the planning, the remembering, the soft background labor that keeps a life running, and they never quite noticed. You didn't complain. You held it until you couldn't, and when you finally said 'I'm tired', they looked at you as though you'd changed the rules mid-game. Being taken for granted by someone you'd never call unkind is a confusing hurt. The stability is what pulls. With them, the ground didn't shift. Name your work as you do it. 'I booked the dentist for you.' 'I sorted the bills.' Not as a complaint. As information. People can't appreciate what they don't know exists.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gi, you did so much quietly. Next time, say it out loud.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Mu's 'don't worry' has never once stopped a worrier from worrying.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Same landscape. Learn each other's weather.

gi-earth.title: Two gardens sharing a fence
gi-earth.text: Two Gi Earths together are the kindest couple at every dinner party, and the most tired couple on the way home. You both say yes to everyone. You both check if the other has eaten. 'Home safe?' 'Did you eat?' 'I bought the thing.' Sweet, careful, practical love. The trouble is that neither of you likes confrontation, so small resentments were composted rather than discussed. You both over-planned and under-enjoyed: holidays became checklists, weekends became errands, and a city break had a spreadsheet with tabs. And when both of you worried about the same thing at the same time, nobody was left to say 'it's going to be okay.' You took such good care of each other's logistics that nobody took care of the feelings. The comfort is what pulls you. It was the safest you've ever felt. Practice saying the hard thing early, kindly. 'I'm annoyed, can we talk?' And send one message a day that isn't a task. Gardens need sunshine, not just weeding.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: 'Did you eat?' 'Did you?' 'Yes.' 'Me too.' Riveting. Romantic, though.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You cared for each other so well. Care for the feelings too.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: One message a day that isn't a task. Start today.

gyeong-metal.title: Fertile ground for raw ore
gyeong-metal.text: You were the soil that shaped the steel. Your Gyeong Metal ex grew stronger with you: you supported, encouraged, made the home that made their big pushes possible. 'Done. Coming home,' they'd text. 'Great, dinner's ready, how did it go?' you'd reply. They often didn't answer the question. Over time, they took your support for granted and steamrolled your quieter opinions. You held back your worries to avoid their impatience, and resented it later. Their harsh words wounded you more than they knew, because you kept them inside. Slowly you started to feel less like a partner and more like staff. You helped build someone who forgot to look back at the builder, and that's a lonely place to stand. The strength is what you miss. Next to them, you felt protected and proud. Say what you need instead of hinting. 'I need you to ask about my day.' 'That comment hurt.' Practice with people who are safe. Your voice matters as much as your help.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gi, you were a partner, not staff. Say it louder.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gyeong's 'fine' was not an answer to 'how did it go?'

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Patience that shapes strength. Make sure it's thanked.

sin-metal.title: The jeweler's workbench
sin-metal.text: You and your Sin Metal ex were two perfectionists sharing a workbench, and you both had very careful hands. They critiqued; you worried about the critique; both of you lost sleep. A three-line text could take ten minutes to write on both ends. You found them cold or demanding at times. They found you fussy or anxious. Neither of you likes confrontation, so issues festered under very good manners, and the politeness became its own kind of distance. Nobody ever shouted, and still it felt like walking on glass. What pulls you back is the care in it. You both took love seriously, and they noticed your effort in a way not everyone does. Lower the stakes. Send the silly text. Make a small mistake on purpose and see that nothing breaks. Two careful people need someone to be a little careless now and then, and it may as well be you. Your standards are a gift. They just weren't meant to be aimed at the person you were trying to rest with.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: A three-line text took ten minutes. On both ends. Exhausting.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Sin gave notes where a hug was needed.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Send the silly one. Nobody ever broke up over a dumb meme.

im-water.title: The garden and the flood
im-water.text: You were the garden and they were the flood. Your Im Water ex was exciting, unpredictable, big-hearted and chaotic. Plans changed constantly. Moods rolled in like weather. You need plans the way plants need sunlight, and every sudden change made you anxious. You worried; they dismissed your worry as overthinking. You tried to organize their life a little, and they hated being managed. They sent bursts of messages, then went silent for days, and you counted the silence, hour by hour. Over time, you felt drained, like a garden after a storm. You poured care into someone who kept washing it away. Their aliveness is the hook. They made your careful life feel adventurous. Stop counting. Notice the urge to check whether someone has replied, and do something nourishing instead. And when you worry, say it as a need, not a forecast: 'I feel calmer when I know the plan.' Your steadiness is precious. It doesn't need to be spent keeping up with someone else's tide.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gi, stop counting the hours between texts. You deserve peace.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Im kept missing the actual question. Answering it is a whole skill.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Care meets chaos. Both can grow. Just separately sometimes.

gye-water.title: Rain on the garden bed
gye-water.text: You tried to organize the rain. Your Gye Water ex was gentle, moody, poetic. You asked practical questions; they answered with feelings or poems or silence. When their mood shifted, you felt anxious and tried to fix it; they felt managed. Both of you avoid conflict, so nothing got said clearly, and things stayed murky. You thought they were unreliable. They thought you were controlling. The classic moment: you asked 'what's wrong?' and they said 'nothing', and both of you knew it was something, and neither of you went further. Two gentle people stuck in fog, each waiting for the other to clear it. The tenderness is what pulls you. They softened your practical world. Stop trying to manage moods, including your own. Let someone feel sad without needing to solve it. Ask 'do you want help or company?' and accept the answer. That question alone would have changed so many evenings. Your care is real. It just doesn't always have to arrive as a plan.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: 'What's wrong?' 'Nothing.' The most expensive word in your relationship.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gi, ask 'help or company?' and trust the answer.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gye needed to answer the question first, then send the poem.
